Now we ask a quieter question. Suppose a quantity changes over an interval. What single number best represents it?

If a car’s velocity changes during a trip, we can still ask for its average velocity. If a temperature changes during a day, we can still ask for the average temperature. If a probability is spread over many possible outcomes, we can still ask for the expected outcome.
The integral answers all of these by the same idea:

exercise.title: Why does a continuous function reach its average value?

statement.p: The average value theorem says there is some c in [a,b] with f(c)=f_{\text{avg}}. In your own words, why is continuity needed for that guarantee, and what would go wrong if the graph were allowed to jump over its average height?

hint.p: A continuous function on a closed interval attains its min and max, so its average is trapped between them. The Intermediate Value Theorem then supplies a height equal to that average.

subsection.p: In words:
subsection.md: \text{A continuous function reaches its average value somewhere.}

paragraphs.title: Idea of the proof
paragraphs.p: Because f is continuous on [a,b], the Extreme Value Theorem says that f has an absolute minimum m and an absolute maximum M on the interval.

Thus the average value lies between the minimum and the maximum. Since f is continuous, the Intermediate Value Theorem says that f takes every value between m and M. Therefore f takes its average value at some point c.

paragraphs.title: Why continuity matters
paragraphs.p: The average value can exist even when the function is not continuous. But without continuity, the function may not actually equal its average anywhere.
But f(x) is only 0 or 1. It is never equal to \frac12.

exercise.title: Why is the average value of a function an integral divided by a length?

statement.p: A finite average adds values and divides by how many there are. In your own words, why does a continuous function on [a,b] need \frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b f(x)\,dx instead, and what is being added in the numerator?

hint.p: There are infinitely many values, so we imitate the finite average with a Riemann sum. The integral accumulates the values; dividing by the length of the interval turns that total into an average height.

warning.title: Warning
warning.p: A density value is not a probability. A density measures probability per unit length. Only an integral of density over an interval gives probability.

exercise.title: Why is a density value not a probability?

statement.p: A probability density can be larger than 1, even though a probability cannot. In your own words, why does p(x) measure probability per unit length, and why is only an integral of density over an interval a probability?

hint.p: Units matter: density times length gives probability. A tall spike on a short interval can still enclose area less than 1.

subsection.p: The expected value is the balance point of the probability distribution. It is the probability version of center of mass.

exercise.title: Why is expected value the probability version of center of mass?

statement.p: The expected value is E[X]=\int_a^b x\,p(x)\,dx. In your own words, why is x\,p(x)\,dx a small contribution to an average outcome, and why is this the same averaging idea as weighting position by mass?

hint.p: The small probability near x is about p(x)\,dx. Multiplying by the outcome x and adding produces a balance point of the distribution.

This integral has a perfectly clear meaning: it is an area, and therefore a probability.
But there is a surprise. The function
does not have an elementary antiderivative. That means no combination of the usual functions from algebra, trigonometry, exponentials, and logarithms gives an exact antiderivative.
So probability leads naturally to integrals that are meaningful but not elementary.
For the standard normal distribution, we define the accumulation function
The infinite endpoint will be made precise later when we study improper integrals. For now, the meaning is this: \Phi(z) is the probability that a standard normal variable is at most z.
The values of \Phi are found by numerical integration, tables, or technology.

note.title: What probability teaches us
note.p: A definite integral may have an exact meaning even when no elementary antiderivative exists. The integral can define a new function.

subsection.p: Average value and probability both use integrals to summarize spread-out information. The next section changes the geometry again. Instead of adding vertical strips, slices, or forces, we add tiny pieces of a curve itself.
